title: RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory

analysis.tldr: RippleMem treats long-term memory access as evidence completion: first-hop memories become anchors that guide bounded local expansion toward missing support instead of ending retrieval at the initially matched records.
analysis.problem: When answer evidence is distributed across sessions, one-shot retrieval can surface a relevant but incomplete memory, while unguided graph expansion can return nearby yet non-supporting memories.
analysis.core_idea: Construct cue-rich event memories linked by sparse semantic and structural associations, perform hybrid first-hop recall, let a recollection controller decide whether support is missing and choose memory anchors plus a missing-support target, then expand only around those anchors and assemble a budgeted evidence set.

memory_design.write: Process overlapping dialogue windows with a schema-guided LLM extractor that emits self-contained event memories containing a canonical restatement, dense vector, participants, locations, and temporal cues when grounded.
memory_design.organize: Maintain a sparse event-centric graph with typed semantic edges and structural edges based on shared participant/location/time cues; incremental insertion uses bounded semantic and cue-based candidate pools.
memory_design.read: Use semantic, lexical, and structured-cue recall for the initial evidence set; if evidence is incomplete, a controller selects anchors and a missing-support target, performs bounded anchor-local expansion over typed graph edges, then orders and budgets the assembled evidence.
memory_design.update_forget: New event memories and graph edges are added incrementally. The paper does not introduce long-horizon aging, deletion, privacy-preserving forgetting, or conflict-repair policies.

compared_to: RF-Mem under matched RippleMem memory units and per-question evidence budget, isolating the access strategy more cleanly than cross-system comparisons
SimpleMem and long-term memory systems including Mem0, Zep, LightMem, MemOS, and EverMemOS
structured/associative access systems including REMem, MemGAS, and M-Flow
analysis.evidence: On LoCoMo, RippleMem reaches 87.14% LLM-judge accuracy versus 83.83% for RF-Mem under matched memory units/evidence budget. The access ablation is diagnostic: removing graph expansion drops judge accuracy to 83.12, removing structural cues to 83.83, and removing planned recollection to 84.35. On LongMemEval-S it reaches 84.80% in the SimpleMem-aligned setting and 86.60% in the EverMemOS-aligned setting; multi-session accuracy improves from 60.92 to 78.20 versus SimpleMem and from 73.68 to 80.45 versus EverMemOS. Graph construction is reported at 117.5 s and 87K tokens per LoCoMo dialogue, about 30x less time than the compared Mem0g/Zep graph-construction settings.
analysis.why_it_matters: RippleMem supplies a stronger answer to the current raw-record-versus-structure debate: structure earns complexity when it changes the read operator from isolated matching into controlled evidence completion, and the matched RF-Mem comparison suggests that the gain is not only from better memory extraction.
limitations: Evaluation is primarily text conversational QA rather than acting agents, multimodal memory, or tool-state reuse.
Memory extraction, query analysis, and recollection planning still require LLM calls, so the low build cost relative to graph baselines does not imply low end-to-end query latency.
The reported recollection budget is only one additional round, leaving scaling behavior under deeper iterative recollection unclear.
Continuously growing histories, aging, deletion, privacy, and contradiction repair are not stress-tested.
